module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Wolstenholme Prime

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolstenholme_prime)
-/

@[expose] public section


namespace WolstenholmePrime

/--
Wolstenholme's theorem states that any prime $p > 3$ satisfies $\binom{2p-1}{p-1} \equiv 1 (\pmod{p^3})$.

Formal proof linked here provided by AlphaProof.
*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolstenholme%27s_theorem)
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 11, formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
"https://github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures/blob/d833ed31d82693f10bed7a4c9ac329545b556a03/FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/WolstenholmePrime.lean#L34"]
theorem wolstenholme_theorem (p : ℕ) (h : p > 3) (hp : Nat.Prime p) :
    (2 * p - 1).choose (p - 1) ≡ 1 [MOD p ^ 3] := by
  sorry


/--
A prime $p > 7$ is called a *Wolstenholme prime* if $\binom{2p-1}{p-1} \equiv 1 (\pmod{p^4})$.
-/
def IsWolstenholmePrime (p : ℕ) : Prop :=
  p > 7 ∧ p.Prime ∧ (2 * p - 1).choose (p - 1) ≡ 1 [MOD p ^ 4]

/--
Two known Wolstenholme primes: 16843 and 2124679.

Formal proof linked here provided by AlphaProof
-/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem wolstenholme_prime_16483 : IsWolstenholmePrime 16843 := by
  unfold IsWolstenholmePrime Nat.ModEq
  refine ⟨by norm_num, by norm_num, ?_⟩
  native_decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem wolstenholme_prime_2124679 : IsWolstenholmePrime 2124679 := by
  unfold IsWolstenholmePrime Nat.ModEq
  refine ⟨by norm_num, by norm_num, ?_⟩
  native_decide

/--
Equivalently, a prime $p > 7$ is a Wolstenholme prime if it divides the numerator of the Bernoulli number $B_{p-3}$.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem wolstenholme_bernoulli (p : ℕ) : IsWolstenholmePrime p ↔
    (p > 7) ∧ Nat.Prime p ∧ ↑p ∣ (bernoulli' (p - 3)).num := by
  sorry

/--
Another equivalent definition is that a prime $p > 7$ is a Wolstenholme prime
if it $p^3$ divides the numerator of the harmonic number $H_{p-1}$.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem wolstenholme_harmonic (p : ℕ) : IsWolstenholmePrime p ↔
    (p > 7) ∧ Nat.Prime p ∧ ↑(p ^ 3) ∣ (harmonic (p - 1)).num := by
  sorry

/--
It is conjectured that there are infinitely many Wolstenholme primes.

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolstenholme_prime#Expected_number_of_Wolstenholme_primes)
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem wolstenholme_prime_infinite :
    {p : ℕ | IsWolstenholmePrime p}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end WolstenholmePrime

reformulations.difference: The Lean uses Mathlib's `bernoulli'` (the convention B'_1 = +1/2), not `bernoulli` (B_1 = -1/2). It also puts `p > 7` on the right-hand side, while Wikipedia's Bernoulli definition ('a prime p that divides the numerator of B_{p-3}') has no lower bound.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For p > 7 we have p - 3 >= 5, so p - 3 != 1. Then `bernoulli_eq_bernoulli'_of_ne_one` gives bernoulli (p-3) = bernoulli' (p-3); the two sequences differ only at index 1. No prime <= 7 meets the Bernoulli condition: with truncated subtraction the indices are 0, 0, 2 and 4, and B_0 = 1, B_2 = 1/6, B_4 = -1/30 all have numerator +-1. So the guard excludes nothing. Scratch theorem `ber_equiv` proves that the Lean statement is equivalent to `∀ p, p.Prime → (IsWolstenholmePrime p ↔ ↑p ∣ (bernoulli (p - 3)).num)`, using only the standard axioms. For p >= 11 the equivalence is exactly McIntosh 1995's Corollary, (i) <-> (ii). It is also consistent with Glaisher's congruence C(2p-1,p-1) ≡ 1 - (2/3) p^3 B_{p-3} (mod p^4). Numerically, all primes 11..12000 and both known Wolstenholme primes agree.

reformulations.difference: The right-hand side has a `p > 7` guard. Wikipedia's harmonic definition ('a prime p such that H_{p-1} ≡ 0 mod p^3, i.e. p^3 divides the numerator of H_{p-1} in lowest terms') has no lower bound.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: No prime <= 7 satisfies p^3 | num(H_{p-1}): H_1 = 1, H_2 = 3/2, H_4 = 25/12 and H_6 = 49/20 have numerators 1, 3, 25 and 49, which 8, 27, 125 and 343 do not divide. So the guard excludes nothing. Scratch theorem `harm_equiv` proves that the Lean statement is equivalent to `∀ p, p.Prime → (IsWolstenholmePrime p ↔ ↑(p ^ 3) ∣ (harmonic (p - 1)).num)`, using only the standard axioms. The underlying equivalence is the classical one Zhao cites: H_{p-1} ≡ -(p^2/3) B_{p-3} (mod p^3). Numerically, all primes 11..12000 agree, and the literal Lean expression holds at 16843.

sources_consulted: R. J. McIntosh, On the converse of Wolstenholme's Theorem, Acta Arith. 71 (1995) 381-389, http://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/ksiazki/aa/aa71/aa7144.pdf (definition of Wolstenholme primes; Theorem 2; Corollary (i)<->(ii) for p >= 11; infinitude conjecture and heuristic)

J. Zhao, Bernoulli numbers, Wolstenholme's theorem, and p^5 variations of Lucas' theorem, J. Number Theory 123 (2007), arXiv:math/0303332 (abstract page and LaTeX e-print; introduction: H_1(p-1) = 0 mod p^3 iff p divides numerator of B_{p-3})
https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.11157 (Booker, Hathi, Mossinghoff, Trudgian, Wolstenholme and Vandiver primes, Ramanujan J. 58 (2022): abstract, current search status)
review.notes:
Checked every declaration against its source.
- wolstenholme_theorem: 'p > 3 and prime' is the same as Wikipedia's 'prime p >= 5'. Checked by #eval: the mod p^3 congruence holds for all primes 5..397 and fails for 2 and 3.
- IsWolstenholmePrime: matches Wikipedia's binomial definition literally (p > 7, prime, C(2p-1,p-1) ≡ 1 mod p^4). McIntosh defines it with no p > 7, which is equivalent: proved by `decide` that no prime <= 7 satisfies the p^4 congruence.
- The two test theorems: closed by native_decide (#print axioms confirms), and the module builds.
- wolstenholme_prime_infinite: the conjecture as posed by Wikipedia and McIntosh. It is still open; Booker et al. 2022 only extended the search to 10^11.

Lean computations: for all primes 11 <= p < 12000 the three conditions agree. They are the p^4 binomial condition, the Bernoulli condition (computed via sum_{a<p} a^{p-3} ≡ p*B_{p-3} mod p^2) and the harmonic condition (H_{p-1} mod p^3). All three hold at 16843 and 2124679. Neither prime satisfies the p^5 binomial condition. The literal expression `((16843^3 : ℕ) : ℤ) ∣ (harmonic 16842).num` evaluates to true.

Not reported as findings (naming or docstring slips, mathematics intact):
- The test `wolstenholme_prime_16483` has a digit swap in its name; the statement correctly uses 16843.
- That test's docstring says 'Formal proof linked here provided by AlphaProof', but there is no link and the proof is inline native_decide.
- The docstring of wolstenholme_harmonic has a grammar slip: 'if it $p^3$ divides'.

The `formal_proof using formal_conjectures` link on wolstenholme_theorem points to a fork (github.com/mo271/formal-conjectures). I did not open it, because of the rule against consulting the formal-conjectures repository on GitHub. The statement itself is the standard, true theorem.
